c.v: Step and counter flashing

items.v: — Step and counter flashing weaves one metal piece per shingle course against a sidewall or chimney, then caps the step pieces with a separate counter flashing set into the masonry; a continuous one-piece strip is a defective installation, per InterNACHI and shingle-manufacturer guidance.

c.v: Valley flashing

items.v: — Valley flashing lines the channel where two roof planes meet, the transition that concentrates the most runoff on a roof, with a self-adhered ice-and-water shield under the metal that self-seals around fasteners, per ASTM D1970. An open valley leaves the valley metal exposed, and open-valley metal must be at least 24 inches wide, per IRC Section R905.2.8.2, while a closed-cut or woven valley covers the lining with shingles; valley repairs follow the method already on the roof.

c.v: Apron and drip edge flashing

c.v: Kickout and diverter flashing

sections.heading: What Are the Common Problems With Roof Flashing?

c.v: The common problems with roof flashing are rust and corrosion, thermal cracking, failed sealant, cracked pipe boots, and missing or short flashing pieces, and Newark's freeze-thaw winters speed up every one of them.

runs.v: Deteriorating flashing is a major source of leaks in Newark buildings, many of which still carry flashing as old as the roof or older, and expert roof repair starts where the water gets in, not where it shows up.
Rust, Corrosion, and Thermal Cracking

Common issues with roof flashing include rust and corrosion: galvanized steel rusts once its zinc coating wears through, and dissimilar metals fastened together corrode each other. Thermal expansion and contraction can cause cracking in metal flashing, because dark shingles can exceed 160°F on a summer afternoon and cool sharply overnight. Corrosion-resistant materials such as aluminum and copper are recommended for flashing, and debris and rust must be cleared before a flashing leak can be fixed effectively; new metal set against rusted metal fails at the joint.
Failed Sealant and Caulk-Only Repairs

Improper sealants lead to rapid failure in flashing systems. Sealant alone dries and cracks within a few years, and roof cement smeared over a lifted flashing edge traps water behind it. A repair that depends on caulk instead of lapped metal is a temporary patch, not a permanent repair.
Cracked Pipe Boots at Plumbing Vents

Pipe boot flashings seal plumbing vent penetrations, and they are often the first flashing to fail on a newer roof: the rubber collar hardens from UV exposure and freeze-thaw cycles and splits around the pipe while the shingles still look sound. Roof vent repair replaces the failed housing or flashing at the penetration, and pipe boots with a cracked collar are replaced, not caulked.
Missing Kickouts and Short Drip Edge

Kickout flashing diverts water away from walls at roof intersections; without one, the eave dumps water behind the siding. A drip edge that is missing or too short lets water wick behind the gutter into the fascia and the deck edge, which is why IRC Section R905.2.8.5 requires drip edge to extend at least 2 inches onto the deck at eaves and rakes.
Freeze-Thaw Cycles and Summer Heat on a Newark Roof

Newark experiences freeze-thaw cycles that impact flashing performance: a Newark roof goes through dozens of freeze-thaw cycles each winter, commonly estimated at 30–50, and water that freezes in a small gap at a flashing lap expands and widens it. Properly installed roof flashing is crucial to combat heavy rainfall and snow loads, because snow melting against a wall or chimney feeds water into the same laps for days. A roof inspection should occur twice a year, in spring and fall, and routine inspections after a storm catch flashing issues early and prevent leaks. A thorough roof inspection covers every penetration, not just the one that leaked, and regular inspections prevent costly roof repairs later.

sections.heading: Flashing Repair or Full Roof Replacement? What Newark Homeowners Should Weigh

c.v: Repair the flashing when the leak stays at one transition and the roof around it is sound; replace the roof when the damage is widespread or the roof is near the end of its life.

runs.v: Contractor-consensus thresholds make the call clearer: replacement makes sense when damage exceeds 25–30% of the roof area or a single repair approaches 50% of replacement cost, and granule loss exceeding 30% indicates a shingle roof past repair.

Flashing can almost always be repaired without a full roof replacement. A failed pipe boot, a lifted apron, or a rusted run of step flashing comes out with the shingle courses around it and goes back as new metal, and whether to reseal or replace flashing depends on the metal: bent, rusted, or caulk-covered flashing gets replaced, while sound metal with a failed sealant joint can be reset and lapped correctly. The roof's condition decides the rest. Asphalt shingles last 20–30 years with proper maintenance, metal roofs can last over 50 years with minimal upkeep, and tile roofs typically last over 50 years with proper care, so a flashing failure on a 25-year-old shingle roof is a different conversation than the same failure on a 10-year-old metal roof.
Flashing on a New Roof Installation

A full roof replacement is the time to replace flashing rather than reuse it. Roof replacement typically involves removing the old roofing material down to the deck, and the process includes a thorough assessment of the roof's condition — decking, ventilation, and every transition — before anything new goes on. Drip edge, valley metal, step flashing, and pipe boots go back new; counter flashing set in sound masonry can sometimes stay if it is not bent or corroded. Roof replacement may involve multiple types of roofing materials, such as a shingle main roof with a low-slope membrane over a rear addition, and the joint between them is exactly where mixed roofs leak. faqs.q: What is roof flashing and why does it leak?

runs.v: Roof flashing is the sheet metal that seals the transitions and penetrations of a roof — chimneys, walls, valleys, skylights, and vent stacks. It deteriorates as the metal corrodes, wind lifts the laps, and the sealant degrades, and the roofing industry estimates that roughly 90–95% of roof leaks originate at flashing details, an estimate attributed to the NRCA.

faqs.q: How is step flashing installed correctly?

runs.v: Step flashing is used where a roof meets a vertical wall or chimney: one separate metal piece per shingle course, each lapping the course below, so water sheds down the roof. IRC Section R905.2.8.3 requires the step-flashing method against a vertical sidewall, with pieces at least 4 inches high and 4 inches wide, and a continuous one-piece strip is defective per InterNACHI and shingle-manufacturer guidance.

faqs.q: Should you repair or replace your roof?

runs.v: Repair the flashing when the leak stays localized to a transition and the surrounding roof covering holds; replace the roof when damage exceeds 25–30% of the roof area or one repair approaches 50% of replacement cost. These thresholds are contractor-consensus standards, not code.

faqs.q: What is a kickout flashing and does code require it?

runs.v: A kickout flashing diverts water away from the wall cladding where a sloped-roof eave meets a vertical sidewall, and IRC Section R903.2.1 requires flashing at that roof-wall intersection. Omitting one sends water behind the siding, causing hidden rot and mold.

runs.v: No. Caulk alone is a temporary flashing repair, because sealant dries and cracks within a few years while properly lapped, corrosion-resistant metal sheds water without relying on the sealant. A proper repair laps the metal to code and adds an ice-and-water shield underneath.
